newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - May 2.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - May 2.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Friday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* Congress and President Bill Clinton worked to strike a five-year deal to balance the budget, with the final disagreements related to the cost and scope of tax cuts.
* Outdoor Systems announced plans to purchase the billboard unit of Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing for $1 billion, news which sent Outdoor's stock higher.
* A purchasing managers survey showed manufacturing strength fell slightly in April although prices stayed subdued.
* News Corp executive Preston Padden, who oversaw the company's bid to build a U.S. satellite-television service resigned, while Rupert Murdoch said he would still try to enter that market.
* Wasserstein Perella held high-level negotiations with Lazard Freres about combining the companies, but Lazard rejected the idea.
* General Motors and Chrysler said car and light-truck sales fell in April while Toyota Motor and Honda Motor reported a surge in sales.
* America Online, CompuServe and Prodigy agreed to settle government allegations that they misrepresented the terms of "free-trial" offers.
* Heavy rains and labor troubles in South and Central America have caused concern about coffee bean supplies and sparked a rise in retail coffee prices.
* The city of San Francisco sued BankAmerica for $12 million, alleging the bank "mishandled" money from city bond sales and covered its actions.
* The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 32.51 points at 6,976.48, on the heels of the week's earlier rally.
* Informix reported a $140.1 million quarterly loss and said its chief financial officer, who had been on the job for three months, resigned.
* A federal judge approved a pact between IBM and the U.S. Justice Department to phase out a 1956 consent decree, ending a case which had curbed IBM's business tactics.
* The profits of many expanding companies would be affected by a proposed accounting rule requiring firms to immediately write off start-up costs.
* Fidelity Investments said it named James Curvey chief operating officer.

* Heard on the Street: Are expensive Nike sneakers no longer cool among the young urban crowd? You might think so, taking a quick glance at the 25 percent drop in Nike's stock price since the February high of 76-3/8.
* Credit markets: The Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into whether underwriters are selling bonds at artificially low yields to keep hefty underwriting fees rolling in.
